title: A Well for the Portrait
premise: Folklorist Wendell Thornbury arrives in the drowned valley village of Harrow's Bend to record songs the locals refuse to sing twice, convinced their fear is mere superstition. When an excavation crew unearths a stone door sealed from the inside, Wendell discovers her own face in a two-hundred-year-old portrait above it — and learns the village has been paying an annual tithe to something beneath, a debt her bloodline founded. As the thing invited in long ago begins wearing the faces of the villagers she's interviewed, Wendell must choose between completing the ritual that would bind it again at the cost of an innocent life, or breaking the covenant and letting it rise. She breaks it, but at dawn she realizes the price: the thing did not die — it left, wearing her name and her voice, while what remains of Wendell is the one sealed behind the door.
about_author: Emrys Montrose is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing parish records in remote coastal villages before turning to fiction. They write horror rooted in folk custom, oral tradition, and the quiet violence of small communities keeping old bargains.

chapters.title: The Song They Won't Sing Twice
chapters.summary: Wendell Thornbury's POV. She arrives in Harrow's Bend by bus, recorder in hand, and coaxes a lullaby from an old woman named Maren Cole — who stops mid-verse, goes white, and refuses to continue. The villagers watch Wendell with something like pity. Emotional beat: confident skepticism meeting the first crack of genuine dread.

chapters.title: Field Notes from a Drowned Valley
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. She archives the partial song, noticing its melody matches a dirge from a neighboring county — transposed, as if sung underwater. The innkeeper warns her gently to leave before 'the lowering.' Emotional beat: intellectual fascination hardening into stubbornness; she books another week.

chapters.title: The Excavation
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV, visiting the reservoir worksite. Crews draining the old well shaft strike a stone door — carved with interlaced figures, its iron ring fused, sealed unmistakably from the inside. The foreman jokes about it; his crew doesn't laugh. Emotional beat: thrill of discovery shadowed by the crew's unspoken terror.

chapters.title: A Face in the Oil Paint
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. In the church vestry she finds a portrait dated 1798: a woman at a well, unmistakably herself — same scar, same eyes. The curate claims it depicts 'the Founder's daughter, Elowen Thornbury.' Emotional beat: vertigo; her rational framework develops its first structural failure.

chapters.title: What Maren Almost Said
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. She presses Maren about the portrait; the old woman describes the tithe — 'one chosen, one given, every lowering' — then clamps her mouth shut as if something listens through her. That night, Wendell hears singing from the dry well. Emotional beat: fear arriving as knowledge she can't unknow.

chapters.title: The Lowering Begins
chapters.summary: Multiple short POVs — foreman, curate, innkeeper. Preparations sweep the village: doors chalked, livestock penned, children's names written on slips and burned. Everyone knows the ritual except Wendell, and no one will explain. Emotional beat: claustrophobic complicity; the village as a single nervous organism.

chapters.title: The Door Is Open
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. At dawn the excavation site stands abandoned, the door hanging open inward — though it was sealed from within. Cold air breathes out of the shaft, carrying the completed verse of Maren's lullaby. Emotional beat: the moment skepticism dies; Wendell descends one step and retreats.

chapters.title: Interviews with the Borrowed
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. Villagers begin speaking in voices not their own — the foreman recites her own childhood address; the innkeeper hums her mother's tune. Each says some variation of 'you were invited too.' Emotional beat: paranoia; identity itself becomes unreliable terrain.

chapters.title: Elowen's Ledger
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV, searching the vestry archives. She finds Elowen Thornbury's 1798 ledger: the founding family summoned something to end a famine, and the price was a tithe of faces — the thing wears the given, and the village forgets them. Emotional beat: horrified comprehension; her bloodline wrote this contract.

chapters.title: The Tithe Falls Due
chapters.summary: Curate's POV. He reveals to Wendell that the reservoir project broke the seal early, and the covenant demands satisfaction now: one chosen by the thing itself. The chalked names on his door include hers. Emotional beat: dread sharpening into betrayal — the village has known all along.

chapters.title: Maren's Bargain
chapters.summary: Wendell and Maren's shared scene, mostly Maren's voice. Maren confesses she was chosen fifty years ago and bought her life by promising 'the founder's return' — meaning Wendell. Her guilt is forty years deep. Emotional beat: grief and fury entangled; Wendell understands she was delivered here.

chapters.title: Nightfall at the Wellhead
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. She tries to flee; every road out of the valley loops back to the well. The village lights go out one by one, and the singing rises from below in dozens of stolen voices — including, now, her mother's. Emotional beat: trap closing; isolation complete.

chapters.title: The Thing That Wears Faces
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV, at the shaft mouth. It rises partway: a figure assembled from the taken, wearing Elowen's face over its own absence. It speaks with Wendell's voice, offering a trade — the ritual can be completed with any willing vessel. Emotional beat: seduction of the bargain; power dangled like bait.

chapters.title: The Curate's Choice
chapters.summary: Curate's POV. He offers himself instead, believing sacrifice will restore the old order and his standing. The thing accepts his approach — and simply takes his face mid-sentence, leaving him hollow but alive, smiling wrong. Emotional beat: the corruption of power; even devotion becomes currency it spends.

chapters.title: Ritual of the Second Sealing
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. In Elowen's ledger she finds the binding rite: it requires a Thornbury's willing consent, spoken at the threshold, and it does not free the vessel afterward — it seals them inside with the thing. Emotional beat: cold clarity; every exit costs a self.

chapters.title: What Was Invited In
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV, final revelations. She realizes the original invitation never ended — the door was sealed from inside because Elowen went in willingly to contain it, and every 'lowering' since was maintenance, not worship. Wendell is not collateral; she is the scheduled successor. Emotional beat: terrible inheritance accepted.

chapters.title: The Village Decides
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV. The villagers, led by the hollow-smiling curate, gather to deliver Wendell to the well — gently, apologetically, certain it is mercy. Maren turns against them at the last moment, buying Wendell an hour with the only song sung twice. Emotional beat: collective evil rendered banal; one act of defiance.

chapters.title: Descent
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. She goes down the shaft not as prey but as negotiator, carrying the ledger, the recorder, and Maren's completed song. The dark is full of the taken, murmuring her name in voices she loves. Emotional beat: courage stripped of heroism — she is terrified and going anyway.

chapters.title: The Bargain at the Threshold
chapters.summary: Wendell and the thing, direct confrontation. It offers her survival: walk away, let it wear the village, live as herself. She pretends to consent, speaks the binding words at the threshold, and the thing seizes her — but the rite requires willingness, and hers was false. Emotional beat: climax; wit and sacrifice colliding at the door.

chapters.title: Sealed from the Inside
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV, fading. The binding half-holds: the thing cannot leave wearing her, so it takes the next best thing — her name, her voice, her face's memory — and pours past her into the world above as the door slams. Wendell remains in the dark with the taken, whole, conscious, sealed. Emotional beat: victory inverted into entombment.

chapters.title: Sunrise, and Someone Singing
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. Dawn comes; the village wakes remembering nothing, the well filled with concrete by men who don't know why. A woman matching Wendell's description boards the morning bus, humming a lullaby perfectly — and Maren, watching, feels the wrongness like a stone in her chest. Emotional beat: ambiguous dread; survival achieved, identity stolen.

chapters.title: A Well for the Portrait
chapters.summary: Epilogue, split between the impostor-Wendell's smooth public lecture on folklore and brief, rhythmic cuts to the real Wendell in the dark, recording songs with no one left to hear them — keeping herself real by naming what was taken. Final image: the portrait in the vestry, its painted eyes now closed. Emotional beat: haunting resolution; the price of survival paid in perpetuity.
